claims.text: Maintenance of a single-phase solid solution from 473 to 1923 K is governed by kinetic limitations on atomic diffusion.
Kinetic limitations prevent thermodynamic phase separation during standard operating times.
The nanoparticles initially contain five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios.
The nanoparticles are initially crystallized as a single-phase solid solution.
Heating can initiate atomic diffusion that produces local atomic rearrangement or phase segregation.
High entropy in these nanoparticles raises kinetic barriers to atomic diffusion.
Lattice strain in these nanoparticles raises kinetic barriers to atomic diffusion.
Elevated temperatures produce high thermodynamic driving forces for phase separation.
Raised diffusion barriers slow atomic reordering and phase separation.
Slowed atomic reordering and phase separation maintain the chemical and structural integrity of the single-phase solid solution.
During 30–60 minute holds across the tested temperature regime, the nanoparticles will largely retain their single-phase structure.
Phase separation or compositional inhomogeneity will appear only above a critical temperature or after annealing longer than 30–60 minutes.
The stability prediction is limited to controlled inert or reducing atmospheres.
Changes in atmospheric composition or unanticipated catalytic reactions can alter nanoparticle stability.
The temperature and timescale at which kinetic stabilization fails depend on the constituent metals and their interatomic bonding energies.
